content:
A CSR partnerships page is the page on an NGO's website written for company CSR teams, their foundations and the consultants who advise them. Its purpose is to let a CSR manager decide, in one visit, whether your organisation is eligible, credible and a fit for their company's focus, and then to make the next step easy. For NGO website development in India, it is one of the most valuable pages you can add and one of the most often neglected: many NGOs have a general "Donate" page and a "Partner with us" paragraph, but nothing that answers the specific questions a CSR team must answer before it can recommend you internally. This guide explains what those questions are, what to put on the page, which documents to make available and how, and the mistakes that cost NGOs CSR conversations.

It is written for NGO heads, fundraising and partnerships staff, and trustees. It is not legal or tax advice; for questions about your eligibility under the CSR rules, consult your chartered accountant or legal adviser.

## Why CSR teams need a different page

Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, companies above certain thresholds of net worth, turnover or net profit must spend on CSR activities listed in Schedule VII of the Act, and must report that spending. That makes a CSR partnership a compliance decision as well as a philanthropic one. A CSR manager typically has to:

- Confirm that your organisation is an eligible implementing agency, including that it is registered with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs through Form CSR-1 and holds a CSR registration number.
- Match your work to Schedule VII activities and to the company's own CSR policy and focus areas.
- Show the company's CSR committee evidence of your track record, governance and financial health.
- Plan how the project will be monitored and reported, including, for larger projects, impact assessment requirements.

A general donor page, written to move an individual emotionally, does not help with any of this. A CSR page is closer to a well-organised briefing note.

## Who visits and what they want

| Visitor | What they are looking for |
|---|---|
| CSR manager at a mid-sized company | Eligibility, focus fit, past projects, a contact person, a project they can fund this year |
| CSR head at a large company or its foundation | Governance, scale, audited financials, monitoring capacity, references from other corporate partners |
| CSR consultant or implementing partner | Clear programme descriptions, geographies, budgets per unit, reporting formats |
| Employee volunteering coordinator | Volunteering options, logistics, safeguarding rules |
| Company secretary or finance team | Registration numbers and certificates to verify |

Design the page so each of these can find their answer quickly, usually by scanning headings.

## What to put on the CSR page

### 1. A clear opening statement

Two or three sentences that say what you do, where, for whom and at what scale, followed by a direct invitation to partner. For example: "We run after-school learning centres for children from low-income families in Pune and Satara districts. We work with companies to fund centres, teacher training and digital learning labs, and we report progress every quarter. Talk to our partnerships team about a CSR project for this financial year."

Avoid vague openings such as "Together we can change the world". A CSR manager reading a dozen NGO websites in an afternoon will skip it.

### 2. Eligibility and registrations, in one place

A short, factual panel listing:

- Legal form (trust, society or Section 8 company) and registration number.
- CSR registration number (from Form CSR-1).
- 12A (or 12AB) and 80G registration status and validity dates.
- PAN of the organisation.
- FCRA registration, if you have one and it is relevant (for example for foreign-owned companies' Indian CSR arms, where the source of funds may raise questions; check with your adviser).
- NGO Darpan unique ID, if registered.

Show what the registrations are and their validity periods. Whether to show full certificate images publicly is a judgement call; many NGOs show the numbers on the page and share copies of certificates on request or through a gated document link, which reduces the risk of misuse. Whatever you show must be current: an expired 80G date on a CSR page ends conversations.

The CSR rules have been amended several times, including changes to Form CSR-1 in 2025, and they set conditions such as a minimum track record for certain implementing agencies. Ask your adviser to confirm your eligibility, then state it simply on the page.

### 3. Focus areas mapped to Schedule VII

List your programmes and, for each, the Schedule VII item it falls under in plain words: "Promoting education (Schedule VII, item ii)". This saves the CSR team work and shows you understand their constraints. Do not stretch your work to fit categories it does not fit; experienced CSR teams notice, and a wrong mapping can create problems for the company later.

Also mention any alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals if the company reports against them, but keep the Schedule VII mapping first because it is the legal requirement.

### 4. Partnership options with indicative costs

Many CSR teams want to know what a meaningful project looks like and what it costs before they call. Offer three or four clear options, for example:

- **Fund a programme unit**: one learning centre, one mobile health camp series, one skilling batch, with what is included and the indicative annual cost.
- **Fund a capital need**: a digital lab, a vehicle, a building repair, with an indicative cost range.
- **Multi-year partnership**: for companies wanting a flagship project, with an invitation to discuss.
- **Employee volunteering**: what volunteers do, group sizes and how you manage safety.

Give honest ranges based on your real budgets, and state what is and is not included (staff, materials, monitoring, administrative overheads within the limits that apply). If you cannot publish costs, say "Typical projects range from ₹X to ₹Y; we share detailed budgets on request" with figures your finance team has approved. Never publish numbers you cannot back with a budget.

### 5. Track record with evidence

This is where most CSR pages are weakest. Show:

- **Programme outcomes** you can verify: children enrolled and retained, patients screened, women trained and placed, with the year and how you measured them. Link to your annual reports.
- **Past corporate partners**, with logos only where you have written permission to display them. If a partner prefers not to be named, describe the project without the name.
- **Short case studies**: the problem, what was funded, what happened and how it was reported. One page each, with photos used with consent.
- **Testimonials from CSR partners**, quoted accurately and with permission.

Do not overstate. If an outcome came from a pilot with 40 participants, say so. CSR committees increasingly ask for impact assessments, and claims that do not survive scrutiny damage your reputation with the whole network of people who move between companies and consultancies.

### 6. Governance and financial transparency

Link to the pages that hold:

- Board or trustee names and brief profiles.
- Key policies: conflict of interest, child protection or safeguarding, whistleblowing, anti-harassment, financial controls.
- The last three years of audited financial statements and annual reports.

You probably already have these on an About or Governance page; our guide to the [NGO About and governance page](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-about-governance-page-trustees-team-policies-2026) covers how to present them, and our guide to the [annual report and audited financials page](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-annual-report-audited-financials-page-pdf-2026) explains how to publish the documents so they are easy to find and download. Link to both from the CSR page rather than repeating the content.

### 7. How you monitor and report

Describe your reporting in concrete terms: frequency (monthly, quarterly), format (dashboard, written report, photos and data), what indicators you track, how you handle utilisation certificates, and whether you have worked with third-party impact assessors. If you have a sample report with confidential details removed, offer it on request. This section reassures a CSR team that it will have what it needs for its own annual report and board.

### 8. The process from first call to agreement

A simple numbered list of what happens: an introductory call, a site visit, a proposal with budget, due diligence documents, an agreement or MoU, fund release schedule, reporting. Add realistic timelines if you know them. CSR budgets often follow the financial year, with much of the decision-making in the first half and pressure to commit funds before 31 March, so let visitors know when to approach you.

### 9. A dedicated contact

Name a person (with their role), a direct email address and a phone number. A generic info@ address and a form that goes nowhere loses partnerships. If you use a form, keep it short: name, company, role, email, phone, area of interest, and a free-text field. State when you will reply, and reply on time.

### 10. A downloadable partnership brochure (optional)

A two- to four-page PDF that summarises the page for the CSR manager to forward internally. Keep the web page as the main source; PDFs get outdated. Put the date on the PDF and update it when registrations or figures change.

## Documents: what to publish and what to share on request

CSR due diligence usually involves a standard document list. Our [CSR due diligence checklist for NGOs](/blog/csr-due-diligence-checklist-ngos) covers it in detail. On the website, the practical split is:

| Publish openly | Share on request or via a secure link |
|---|---|
| Registration numbers and validity dates | Copies of certificates (registration, 12A/12AB, 80G, CSR-1 acknowledgement) |
| Annual reports | Board resolutions, detailed project budgets |
| Audited financial statements (summary or full) | Bank details and cancelled cheque |
| Governance and safeguarding policies | KYC of signatories |
| Programme descriptions and outcomes | Beneficiary-level data (never public) |

A secure link can be as simple as a password-protected folder shared after the first call, or a small "partner documents" area on the website. Whatever you use, log who has access and remove it when it is no longer needed.

## Writing for CSR readers

- **Lead with facts, not adjectives.** A line in the form "eight learning centres, 640 children enrolled in 2025-26" is more persuasive than "transforming thousands of lives". Those numbers are only an illustration of the format; use your own verified figures.
- **Use plain headings** that match the questions: "Are we eligible?", "What can you fund?", "How we report".
- **Be specific about geography.** CSR policies often prefer the company's local areas. Name districts and talukas.
- **Show people with dignity.** Photographs of beneficiaries need informed consent, and children's images need particular care. Avoid images that portray people as helpless.
- **Keep it current.** Add the date the page was last reviewed at the bottom.

## Technical details for the website team

- **URL and navigation**: give the page a clear URL such as `/csr-partnerships/` and link it from the main menu (under "Partner with us" or "Support us") and the footer. CSR managers should not have to hunt.
- **Search visibility**: write a title and meta description that name your cause and location ("CSR Partnerships: Education Projects in Pune | [NGO name]"). Companies and consultants search for NGOs by cause and district.
- **Structured data**: use Organization or NGO schema on the site with your legal name, address and contact details; keep it consistent with the page.
- **Forms**: send enquiries to a shared inbox and a CRM or tracker so nothing is lost when a staff member leaves. Protect the form against spam without making it hard for humans.
- **Speed and mobile**: many CSR managers first open your link from a WhatsApp forward on their phone. Test the page on a phone, keep images light and make the contact button easy to tap.
- **Accessibility**: proper heading order, sufficient contrast and descriptive link text ("Download our 2025-26 annual report (PDF, 3 MB)") rather than "click here".
- **Analytics**: track form submissions, brochure downloads and clicks on the email and phone links as key events so you know whether the page produces conversations.

## Common mistakes

1. **No CSR registration number shown**, so the CSR team assumes you are not registered and moves on.
2. **Outdated certificates or validity dates**, especially after 12A/80G re-registration.
3. **Logos of companies that did not agree to be displayed**, or that funded you years ago and are presented as current.
4. **Inflated impact numbers** that do not match the annual report.
5. **No indication of cost**, leaving the CSR manager unable to judge fit.
6. **A contact form that sends to an unmonitored inbox.**
7. **Mixing the CSR page with the individual donation page**, so neither audience is well served. Link between them, but keep them separate.

## How this page fits with the rest of the site

The CSR page sits alongside your donation page, volunteer page and governance pages. If your NGO also runs a corporate employee volunteering programme, consider a dedicated page or portal for it; our guide to [CSR volunteer portals](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-csr-volunteer-portals-2026) covers that. Link from the CSR page to individual programme pages so a CSR manager can read more about a specific project; our guide to [building programme pages that donors and CSR teams trust](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-programme-pages-our-work-impact-donors-csr-2026) explains what each of those pages should contain.

## An illustrative example

Consider a Pune-based NGO running vocational training for young women. Its website has a donation page and a one-line "Corporate partners welcome" note. After adding a CSR page with its CSR registration number, a Schedule VII mapping, three costed partnership options, two short case studies and a named partnerships manager, it starts receiving enquiries that already reference a specific option, which shortens the first call. This is an invented example to illustrate the approach, not a report on a real organisation.

## Frequently asked questions

### What should an NGO's CSR page include?
A clear statement of your work and geography, eligibility details including your CSR registration number and 12A/80G status, programmes mapped to Schedule VII, partnership options with indicative costs, evidence of track record, links to governance and audited financials, your reporting approach, the partnership process and a named contact.

### Does an NGO need CSR-1 registration to receive CSR funds?
Implementing agencies carrying out CSR activities on behalf of companies are generally required to register with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs by filing Form CSR-1 and obtain a CSR registration number. Eligibility conditions apply, so confirm your position with your chartered accountant or legal adviser.

### Should we publish our 12A and 80G certificates on the website?
Publish the registration numbers and validity dates so CSR teams can check eligibility quickly. Many NGOs share copies of the certificates on request or through a secure link to reduce misuse. Keep all dates current.

### How do companies find NGOs for CSR partnerships?
Through referrals, CSR consultants, government and private NGO directories, and web searches by cause and location. A clear CSR page with your cause and district in its title and headings helps you appear in those searches and gives a good impression when someone forwards your link.

### Can we show corporate partner logos on our website?
Only with the company's permission, and only for genuine partnerships. Indicate the period of the partnership if it has ended. Using logos without consent can damage relationships and may raise legal issues.
